item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian cargo ship hit by drone in Baltic Sea as Finland PM says conflict ‘spilling over’
item.description:
Vessel erupts in flames after strike in Gulf of Finland; Nato vows to defend ‘every inch’ of Polish territory. What we know on day 1,733

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.

Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”

The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.

“I can guarantee ⁠that Nato will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said in Warsaw on Saturday, after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in its territory on Friday. Poland accused the Kremlin of “intentional provocation” after the incident, as it occurred near where thousands of European troops allied with Ukraine were holding training exercises.

A meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles. “In the near future, we ​will receive ​strong support from our NATO ​allies to bolster the protection of our eastern ​border,” Polish defence minister ‌Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote ​on ​X on Saturday.

In Kyiv, residents say they are unbothered by Russian attacks on the city’s bridges, as Moscow tries to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, Dan Sabbagh reports. Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population. Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

item.title: Why Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm is the focus of a widening probe in the House
item.description:
A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.

The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether U.S. President Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.

The investigation was opened over the summer

Both Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital, which is based in Palm Beach, Florida, deny any wrongdoing.

The letters ramp up an investigation that Raskin opened in August into Trump Jr.’s firm, which he said “suddenly struck investment gold” after naming the president’s son as a partner in 2024. As one of the lawmakers who will be spearheading Democrats’ oversight of the Trump administration when they take control of Congress in January, Raskin has said that uncovering information about bribery and financial corruption will be among his top priorities.

Trump Jr. has repeatedly rejected accusations that he has exploited government access for profit. At an Axios event last week, he acknowledged that he understood people’s corruption concerns, but said that they weren’t accurate, noting he has been an investor for decades.

“I can see what they are saying. It doesn’t make it so,” he said. “The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb and wait, you know, eight years — in this case 12 years — till we’re out of the political game, it’s not real.”

Trump Jr. and the firm deny any wrongdoing

1789 Capital also has forcefully denied claims of wrongdoing. In a letter to Raskin in September, the company’s lawyers defended the firm’s investment thesis as predating Trump’s administration and said that while it “welcomes legitimate congressional oversight,” it “has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship.”

On Monday, the company’s attorney, Bill Burck, said the September letter explained flaws in Raskin’s understanding, but Raskin “never bothered to reply.”

“Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here, but persists in his tall tales against 1789,” Burck said. “These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence.”

‘Serendipitous timing’ of investments, Raskin says in letters

The firm was founded in 2022 and Trump Jr. was announced as a partner in November 2024.

In his letters to the four companies obtained by The Associated Press, Raskin outlined how federal policies or contracts had benefited their businesses and claimed that 1789 Capital had suspiciously “serendipitous timing” when it invested in them.

Hadrian Automation, he wrote, received nearly $1 billion in U.S. Navy and Army contracts in March — its first-ever federal contracts — after bringing 1789 Capital on as an investor in 2025.

Juul, Raskin wrote, received Food and Drug Administration clearance to keep its electronic cigarette products on the market in July 2025, four months after 1789 Capital had taken a stake in the company.

The congressman wrote that GrabAGun got help from 1789 to go public and put Trump Jr. on its board before the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a proposed rule to ease the process of shipping guns to people’s homes.

Raskin calls Trump administration order ‘blatantly unlawful’

Raskin also raised questions about the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission closing investigations into Polymarket in July 2025, after 1789 Capital already had invested in the prediction market platform.
GrabAGun said in a statement that Raskin’s letter “is a political document, and its allegations are baseless.”

“ATF’s review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun’s only input came through public comments on several of those proposals,” the statement read.

Juul Labs said that it was reviewing its letter closely.

“As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking,” it said in an emailed response.

The other recipients of the letters didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Trump administration has taken steps to push back on the Democrats’ oversight efforts, including an executive order on Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged.

That could complicate compliance with Raskin’s investigation for at least one of the companies, Hadrian Automation, which is a federal contractor.

Raskin has called Trump’s order “blatantly unlawful” and said that public contractors have a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls.”

item.title: Digital Duty of Care Act passes in Australia. Opposition say the law is ‘authoritarian’
item.description:
Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.

The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

Australian online law falls in line with EU and British legislation

The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”

“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.”

The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.

“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

—Rod Mcguirk, Associated Press

item.title: Elon Musk is giving away nearly $18 billion in SpaceX stock. Here’s who can get it
item.description:
Your kid is becoming quite the capitalist.

Every U.S. child with an active Trump account will soon receive two shares of SpaceX, the space exploration company run by Elon Musk. This donation marks the latest in a string of philanthropic initiatives focused on these new types of tax-advantaged investment accounts.

SpaceX announced Wednesday that the company will donate one share of its Class A common stock—currently trading for more than $130 per share—to every currently active Trump account. In turn, CEO Musk will match that donation, which he later confirmed on X.

“Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally,” Musk posted. 

In its official announcement, SpaceX touted its future-focused mission of building new infrastructure that could achieve multiplanetary living. “We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit.”

Here’s what we know about the donations.

MILLIONS OF NEW SHAREHOLDERS

The portfolios of the country’s youngest generation of investors keep getting fatter. Launched earlier this year, Trump accounts allow deposits of up to $5,000 per year for each child until the age of 18 and various billionaires have even thrown some money into the mix.

Musk now joins the likes of Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, who have similarly pledged donations to Trump accounts. The U.S. Treasury Department, too, will make a one-time $1,000 deposit to every child born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028.

The SpaceX shares work a little differently in that the company will transfer one share of its stock to active Trump accounts in December, according to Musk’s post. Nearly 70 million accounts have been created thus far, the White House reported last month, though that’s largely a result of a change by the Treasury to allow for automatic enrollment. 

Musk’s matching donation will come later, he said on X, sometime after mid-June 2027. That’s when a 366-day lockup expires that he agreed to as part of the SpaceX initial public offering earlier this year.

The Starbase, Texas-based company noted that Gwynne Shotwell, its president and chief operating officer, previously pledged with her husband to donate more than 2 million shares to Trump accounts. But there are strict eligibility requirements associated with those donations, which parents can check online.

Combined, the gifts from the company, Musk, and Shotwell could have a value of more than $18 billion given the stock’s current price and if all eligible Trump accounts have been claimed. These donations also do something that’s delving into new territory: They guarantee that potentially millions of Americans will become long-term shareholders of SpaceX. 

YOU GET A STOCK!

Just as Oprah famously announced a new car to every person in her studio audience back in the early 2000s, Musk and other billionaires are saying the same to kids now: “You get a stock!”

But that could create a conundrum of sorts for parents as more and more money is likely to flow into these accounts from billionaires. 

The Treasury recently implemented new rules that allow companies and other donors to gift individual stocks to these accounts, while also limiting trading activity in them, as The Wall Street Journal reported. Children and their parents can neither pick nor reject stocks that are donated to a child’s account—and they can’t sell them for five years.

And yet, there’s free money on the line. If parents don’t claim an account on behalf of their kid, their kid misses out on a potentially lucrative portfolio. Despite the move to automatic enrollment, some manual steps are still required, which means parents need to claim an account by downloading an app from the Trump accounts website. 

Musk couldn’t help but tout the prospects of what that could mean to millions of prospective shareholders—something that resonated with investors, too, as the stock has jumped nearly 5% in the past two days of trading.

“If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy,” Musk posted. “These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them. I recommend holding on to your shares.”

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy criticises Trump for calling Putin his ‘friend’; Kyiv deploys new laser weapon
item.description:
Ukrainian leader likens Putin to Hitler; laser system intercepts Russian drone but not ready for ‘mass deployment’. What we know on day 1,739

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin his “friend”, likening the Russian leader to Adolf Hitler. “Of course it’s up to the president of the United States, but ... it’s strange,” the Ukrainian leader told the BBC in an interview aired on Friday. “He is an aggressor, and a killer... He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody says about Hitler during the second world war, that he’s a good friend. No. He’s not a friend.” Zelenskyy said what was needed was “more progress” and urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow.

Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, according to its state-backed defence group Brave1. An adviser to Zelenskyy, Serhiy Beskrestnov, published footage earlier this week showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system known as Blysk for the “first time”. Agence France-Presse quoted Brave1 as saying on Friday: “Footage recently emerged online showing a Ukrainian laser system being used in combat to intercept an enemy jet-powered drone.” But Brave1 cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”. “Laser air defence remains an experimental technology,” it said, adding that at least seven teams in Ukraine were working on laser weapons.

Ukraine on Saturday reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured. Zaporizhzhia military administration chief Ivan Fedorov said more than 700 Russian drones had been fired at the region over the past 24 hours. Russian authorities said more than 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight, with hundreds aimed at the Moscow region, while the governor of Bryansk region ‌said a Ukrainian drone struck a bus ​in the village of Klimovo, wounding nine people.

A convoy of Russian ships carrying military vehicles bound for Libya has turned around in the Mediterranean after Ukrainian maritime drones sank ⁠a Russian naval warship in Benghazi ⁠port last Sunday, Reuters quoted ​three people from military and security services as saying on Friday. The convoy, which was escorted by the Russian navy frigate Golovko, turned around near the strait of Sicily on the same day as ⁠the attack in Benghazi, said a European military official who had been tracking the convoy. A Ukrainian military intelligence official and a Middle East security official confirmed the flotilla had turned from heading to Libya. Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ukraine has offered ⁠a Black Sea ceasefire to enable food ⁠exports and ⁠passed this ​on to international allies, the foreign minister ⁠said. “We are ready for ⁠a ceasefire. We are ​grateful to ‌India, Turkey and ‌Egypt, which are playing ‌an active and important role in de-escalating tensions in the Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts. ‌We are now awaiting a response from ​Russia,” Andrii Sybiha was cited by public broadcaster Suspilne as saying on Friday. He added that Russia had proposed ⁠Ukraine suspend attacks on the ​Russian ​oil sector under ​the truce, but ​Kyiv ‌would only consider ​this ​as part of a bigger energy ceasefire deal.

Ukraine’s military said on ⁠Friday it ⁠had struck ​a Russian solid ⁠rocket fuel production site ⁠in ​the Tula ‌region south ‌of Moscow ‌overnight. “The plant is the starting point of the ‌missile production chain: it manufactures ​components for plastic explosives and ⁠the polymer used ​to produce ​solid ​propellant for ​Russian ‌ballistic missiles,” ​the ​defence ministry said on Telegram.

Russia’s foreign ministry has accused ⁠Latvia of creating artificial ⁠obstacles ⁠to hinder the ​transit of Russian grain to ⁠global markets, saying the restrictions pose additional risks ⁠to global food security. Ministry ​spokesperson ‌Maria Zakharova ‌claimed in a statement published ‌on the ministry’s website on Friday that Latvia was conducting inspections of Russian grain shipments for allegedly ‌stolen Ukrainian agricultural products and was seeking ways ​to ban Russian grain transit altogether.

item.title: DWP cyber incident ‘probably an attack’, says former UK chief technology officer
item.description:
Government took down pensions and benefits portal on Thursday but said regular payments will not be affected

A serious cyber incident that forced ministers to take down online benefits and pension services was “probably an attack”, the UK’s former chief technology officer has said.

The Department for Work and Pensions took down several systems that appeared to still be offline on Saturday morning. David Knott, who led government technology until December 2025, said much infrastructure was outdated, and underinvestment in defence and increasing sophistication of attacks meant it was only getting more vulnerable.
